blocks.text: 1. SHAP
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354148-795379112.png

Feature Importance and Permutation Importance, both already covered in this module, answer a broadly similar question: which features matter most overall, aggregated across an entire dataset. SHAP, short for SHapley Additive exPlanations, answers a genuinely sharper, more specific question instead: for this one, single, individual prediction, exactly how much did each feature actually contribute, and in which direction, positive or negative?

SHAP is built on Shapley Values, a genuinely rigorous, mathematically grounded concept borrowed directly from cooperative game theory, giving it a level of theoretical justification neither Permutation Importance nor built-in feature importance can claim on their own.
2. The Game Theory Origin
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354149-808072756.png

Shapley Values were originally developed to solve a genuinely different problem entirely: fairly splitting a reward among several players who cooperated together to earn some total combined payout. Given that several players teamed up and earned some total amount together, and each player likely contributed a genuinely different amount to that combined success, how should the total payout be divided among them fairly, in a way that honestly reflects each player's actual individual contribution?

SHAP repurposes this exact same fairness concept directly for machine learning explanation, treating every individual feature in a model as one of these cooperating players, and treating a specific prediction as the payout those features jointly produced together. This reframing is what gives SHAP its name, and its genuine mathematical rigor.
3. Coalitions of Features
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354149-21775008.png

Computing a SHAP value for one specific feature, for one specific prediction, works by considering every possible subset, or coalition, of the other available features. Some of these coalitions happen to include the specific feature being evaluated, and some do not.

For every such coalition, the calculation measures how much the model's prediction actually changes when that specific feature joins the coalition, compared to when it is absent from it. Averaging this change fairly across every single possible coalition, weighting each one appropriately according to the underlying Shapley Value mathematics, produces that specific feature's SHAP value for this one particular prediction, a rigorous, principled measure of its individual contribution.
4. The Additive Property
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354150-597961941.png

SHAP has a genuinely rare, mathematically guaranteed property worth understanding directly: every individual feature's SHAP value for one specific prediction, when summed together across every feature, plus a baseline value representing the model's average prediction across the entire dataset, exactly reconstructs that model's actual, real predicted output for that specific example.

This additive property is not an approximation or a rough guideline; it is a mathematically guaranteed consequence of the underlying Shapley Value calculation, meaning the resulting explanation genuinely, precisely adds up to the actual prediction, with nothing left over and nothing double-counted. This is a genuinely rare guarantee among explainability techniques, and it is one of SHAP's most distinctive, valuable theoretical properties.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This additive guarantee is precisely why SHAP explanations are often visualized as a waterfall, showing the baseline average prediction on one end, each feature's positive or negative contribution stacking up in sequence, and landing exactly on the model's actual final prediction.

blocks.text: 5. Positive and Negative Contributions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354150-205042083.png

A genuinely important property worth stating directly: a feature's SHAP value can be positive or negative, not merely a magnitude the way Permutation Importance's score is. A positive SHAP value means that specific feature pushed this specific prediction higher than the baseline average prediction would otherwise have been.

A negative SHAP value means that specific feature pushed this specific prediction lower than that same baseline. This directional information gives SHAP a genuinely richer explanatory signal than Permutation Importance's magnitude-only score, already covered in its own topic, which reveals only how much a feature mattered overall, never in which specific direction it actually pushed any given individual prediction.
6. Local and Global Views from One Calculation

SHAP values computed for one single, specific prediction constitute what is called a local explanation, exactly the individual-prediction-level detail already emphasized throughout this topic. Averaging the absolute value of every feature's SHAP value across every single prediction in an entire dataset produces a global feature importance ranking too, directly comparable in spirit to the aggregate rankings already covered for Permutation Importance and built-in feature importance.

This is a genuine, practical advantage worth stating directly: SHAP offers both a rich, individual-prediction-level local view and a familiar, aggregate global view, both derived from the exact same underlying calculation, rather than requiring two entirely separate techniques to obtain each kind of view independently.
7. The Real Computational Cost
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354151-458588224.png

Computing exact Shapley Values requires considering every possible coalition of features, already covered in depth earlier in this topic, a quantity that grows combinatorially, exponentially, with the number of features, exactly the same kind of combinatorial explosion already covered for Grid Search back in the Hyperparameter Tuning module.

TreeSHAP offers a genuinely fast, exact shortcut around this exponential cost, but specifically only for tree-based models, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, and similar algorithms already covered throughout the Classification and Ensemble Learning modules, exploiting the specific internal structure those models share. KernelSHAP offers a slower, approximate, but genuinely model-agnostic alternative usable with any other model type at all, trading some computational speed for that broader applicability.

blocks.text: 8. SHAP versus Permutation Importance
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354151-479202894.png

It is worth summarizing the direct comparison against Permutation Importance, already covered in its own topic. Permutation Importance produces one aggregate score per feature across the whole dataset, a magnitude only, with no directional information at all, and it is generally faster to compute, making it a reasonable first choice for a quick, overall importance ranking.

SHAP produces one score per feature, per individual prediction, complete with genuine direction, positive or negative, a considerably richer explanation, at real additional computational cost already covered in the previous section. Neither technique strictly dominates the other; the right choice depends directly on whether an overall, aggregate ranking is sufficient, favoring Permutation Importance, or whether genuinely explaining individual, specific predictions matters for the task at hand, favoring SHAP.

blocks.text: 9. When SHAP Is the Right Explainability Choice

SHAP is the right choice specifically whenever explaining one single, individual prediction genuinely matters, not just understanding overall trends across an entire dataset, exactly the capability neither Permutation Importance nor built-in feature importance can offer on their own. It is also the right choice whenever a rigorous, mathematically guaranteed fair attribution of credit matters, exactly the additive property already covered in depth earlier in this topic, a genuine, real guarantee rather than a rough approximation.

SHAP fits especially well in regulatory or genuinely high-stakes settings requiring a defensible, individually specific explanation for a particular decision, a loan denial or a medical diagnosis being classic, consequential examples where explaining why this specific person received this specific prediction matters enormously, considerably more than understanding aggregate trends across an entire population of predictions.
10. Worked Example
The example below computes SHAP values for a trained Gradient Boosting classifier, examining both an individual prediction explanation and the resulting global feature ranking.

code.content:
import numpy as np
import shap
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(300, 4))
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] * 0.5 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=300) > 0).astype(int)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

model = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# TreeSHAP: fast, exact, specifically for tree-based models like this one
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_test)

# Local explanation: one individual prediction
example_index = 0
print(f"Baseline (expected) prediction: {explainer.expected_value:.4f}")
print(f"SHAP values for example {example_index}: {shap_values[example_index]}")
print(f"Sum of SHAP values plus baseline: {shap_values[example_index].sum() + explainer.expected_value:.4f}")
print(f"Actual model prediction (log-odds): {model.decision_function(X_test[[example_index]])[0]:.4f}")

# Global explanation: average absolute SHAP value per feature
global_importance = np.abs(shap_values).mean(axis=0)
print(f"\nGlobal feature importance (mean absolute SHAP value): {global_importance}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The sum of one example's SHAP values plus the baseline should match that example's actual model prediction almost exactly, a direct, numerical confirmation of the additive property covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: SHAP explains individual predictions, exactly how much each feature contributed and in which direction, not just aggregate trends.
It is built on Shapley Values, a rigorous concept from cooperative game theory for fairly splitting credit among contributors.
A SHAP value is computed by measuring how a prediction changes as a feature joins every possible coalition of other features.
Its additive property is mathematically guaranteed: summed SHAP values plus a baseline exactly reconstruct the actual prediction.
SHAP values carry genuine direction, positive or negative, unlike Permutation Importance's magnitude-only score.
The same calculation offers both a local, individual-prediction view and a global, aggregate importance ranking.
TreeSHAP offers a fast, exact shortcut for tree-based models; KernelSHAP offers a slower, model-agnostic alternative for any model.
It fits explaining individual predictions, rigorous fair attribution, and high-stakes regulatory settings needing defensible explanations.
Next up: LIME, a different, local surrogate-model approach to explaining individual predictions.
